body:
Energy Moves Through an Ecosystem: 1. The sun. 2. From the air and water: "most of the material in a giant oak came from the air and water." 3. A living thing, such as a fungus, bacterium or earthworm, that breaks down dead plants and animals; it returns minerals to the soil so plants can use them again, and without it dead matter would pile up and plants would run out of minerals. 4. "Is eaten by": the grass is eaten by the rabbit, and the rabbit is eaten by the fox; energy and matter move in the direction of the arrows. 5. Deer: herbivore; owl: carnivore; bear: omnivore; mushroom: decomposer. 6. With no foxes to eat them, the rabbits would increase; more rabbits would eat more grass, so the grass would decrease.
Draw a Pond Food Web: A complete web has at least six living things with arrows pointing to the eater, for example algae → tadpole, algae → minnow, tadpole → dragonfly, mosquito → dragonfly, minnow → heron, tadpole (or frog) → heron, and dead matter → bacteria. Algae and cattails are labeled producers; tadpoles, minnows, mosquitoes, dragonflies and herons are consumers; bacteria are decomposers. The spoken explanation follows one path from the sun or a producer to a top consumer.
Should Willow Pond Get Bass?: Either opinion can earn full credit. Strong "no" reasons: bass eat minnows, frogs, tadpoles and dragonfly larvae; the ranger says they could eat most of the minnows in two or three years; minnows and dragonfly larvae eat mosquito larvae, so fewer of them means more mosquitoes, which are already a problem; herons and kingfishers would lose food; nothing in the pond eats full-grown bass. Strong "yes" reasons: visitors for the town and a place for families to fish; possible conditions, such as adding fewer bass or watching the minnow numbers. The food-web reason must show at least two steps (bass eat minnows → fewer minnows eat mosquito larvae → more mosquitoes).
Food Web Check: 1. Grasses and clover; they soak up sunlight to make their own food. 2. Example: clover → mouse → snake → hawk, or grass → grasshopper → snake → hawk. 3. The mouse got energy from clover leaves, seeds or grasshoppers; the grasshoppers got it from grass; the plants got it from the sun. 4. They are decomposers: they break down dead leaves, seeds and animals and return the matter to the soil, where plant roots take it up. Without them, dead things would pile up and the plants would run short of minerals and grow less. 5. Grasshoppers eat grass; when most of them died, much less grass was eaten, so it grew taller. 6. Mice lost some of their food, so there may have been fewer mice or they ate more clover and seeds; snakes also lost grasshoppers and may have had fewer mice to eat, so their numbers might drop too.
Scoring tip: on questions 5 and 6, a correct prediction with no "because" is Developing on reasoning; tracing two links in the web is Proficient.
title: Answer key: Ecosystems and Food Webs
